subject: Solve system of nonlinear equation in Stan

messages.author: 1c55cfd5d20b74c7
messages.subject: Solve system of nonlinear equation in Stan
parts:
Hello Everyone, 

I am wondering is there any function like "nleqslv()" in R to solve system of nonlinear equations? I am doing some Bayesian analysis with HMC in Stan, and the transformed parameters are nonlinear transformation of the parameters. 

Thank you very much!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Solve system of nonlinear equation in Stan
parts:
You can certainly write your own solver — putting into Stan is
a substantially more involved process.  The particularly challenging
part is the efficient calculation of the derivatives (via the implicit
function theorem) and then implementing that generally in Stan.
It’s probably a few months of work to build and test everything,
which is a nontrivial commitment but an excellent project for 
anyone who wants to give it a try!

parts:
On Thursday, March 3, 2016 at 2:26:18 AM UTC-5, Sharon_on_python wrote:
I see. However, I really want to use Stan for the HMC. Can I write my own C++ function to solve system of nonlinear equations and add it to the stan -math library? Any suggestion would be really appreciated! Thank you very much!


Do you have any suggestion to solve this problem?

I agree with Michael that it would be a significant but valuable undertaking (and we would have to come to a consensus on how that function should be called from the Stan Language). But if you were to do it, I would start with the solvers that are already available in Boost or Eigen/unsupported/. In other words, have a functional in Stan Math that takes a vector of vars as starting values and perhaps lower / upper bounds, converts the starting values into a vector of doubles, calls an existing solver to find the root, deals with the implicit differentiation, and returns a vector of vars .

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Solve system of nonlinear equation in Stan
parts:
Michael and Ben are talking about a general solution. If
the nonlinear equations are fixed and you just write a single
solver and can autodiff through a Boost function, it should work;
that's how we started with the diff eq solver. It won't be
as accurate or efficient or general as doing proper analytical
autodiff through the solver.

On the good news front, we just applied for grant funding to
add a root solver and a steady-state solver for ODEs. And
we're working on 1D integrators. So more calc goodness to come,
but probably not for a year or more unless we get some volunteers
with time to do it.

- Bob
